column1: On which two axes is the SOFTENG 761 project assessed?
column2: How well you followed the process, and the quality plus feature richness of your product.

column1: Is delivering a working product sufficient for a good mark?
column2: No. Process followed and product quality both count; "it works" is explicitly not the only requirement.

column1: What is the stated best way to learn Agile?
column2: To do it.

column1: What does Agile and Lean development focus on?
column2: Process and practices, self-organizing teamwork, and project management, to deliver high quality software products.

column1: What standard are students held to in this course?
column2: That of professional software developers, not students.

column1: What framework is the course design based on?
column2: Bloom's Taxonomy of Learning, Revised 2001.

column1: Name Bloom's six levels in order.
column2: Remembering, Understanding, Applying, Analyzing, Evaluating, Creating.

column1: Which Bloom levels does this course weight most heavily?
column2: The top four: Applying, Analyzing, Evaluating and Creating.

column1: What sits at the apex of the course's Bloom mapping?
column2: Creating an Agile Mindset.

column1: Why is a mindset the target rather than knowledge of Agile?
column2: Because the course weights the top of Bloom's taxonomy; 80% is a practical project and there is no final exam.

column1: Is the Scrum Master a project manager?
column2: No. Explicitly not.

column1: What does a Scrum Master actually do?
column2: Champions Agile principles and ensures they are actioned and realised during the project.

column1: What is the structure of an Agile team, per this lecture?
column2: Self-managed, with no team lead.

column1: Is the Scrum Master expected to code more or less than teammates?
column2: Less, because of the extra process responsibilities.

column1: Who should be chosen as Scrum Master?
column2: Someone with Agile experience; failing that, someone with real industry software development experience.

column1: In prescribed Agile, what is a Product Owner?
column2: A software developer.

column1: How does the Product Owner role differ in this course?
column2: It is fused with the client, and the person is often non-technical.

column1: What extra obligation does a non-technical Product Owner create?
column2: You must explain terminology and walk them through expectations.

column1: What does the Product Owner decide each week?
column2: Which features you should implement.

column1: What is your job in relation to the Product Owner's requirements?
column2: To help them find what they need and to help them prioritise features.

column1: What do you do if the Product Owner becomes inaccessible?
column2: Continue the project as previously agreed or as you see fit. You must not stop.

column1: Must a new version ship if the Product Owner is unavailable?
column2: Yes. A new version of the software is required every week regardless.

column1: How many sprints are there, and how long is each?
column2: Seven sprints, each fixed at one week.

column1: Can the sprint length be changed?
column2: No. It is fixed at one week.

column1: Name the five sprint activities in order.
column2: Sprint Planning, Sprint Development, Sprint Review, Sprint Retrospective, Sprint Demo.

column1: What is Sprint 1 called?
column2: The Spike.

column1: What makes the Spike unique among the sprints?
column2: It is the only sprint that does not need to produce new software.

column1: What is the Spike used for?
column2: Understanding what needs doing and deciding the back end, technologies and database technologies.

column1: What two artefacts must the Spike still produce?
column2: Release Planning Parts 1 and 2, and the Product Backlog.

column1: What is the Product Backlog?
column2: The list of features the software should deliver.

column1: What happens in Sprint 2?
column2: System modelling and design, plus the Project Proposal.

column1: Why must Sprint 7 not be treated as a development sprint?
column2: There is no time; it is for polishing, and Part IV project reports are due the same week.

column1: Define imposter syndrome.
column2: The feeling that you are a fake, that you somehow snuck in and do not deserve to be where you are.

column1: What is the claim about how common imposter syndrome is?
column2: It is completely normal; not experiencing it is abnormal.

column1: What does imposter syndrome actually signal, on the reframe given?
column2: That a large volume of new information is coming at you, not that you are inadequate.

column1: What strategy is offered for coping with imposter syndrome?
column2: Do the simplest thing you can do right away.

column1: Why does doing the simplest thing work?
column2: A project is a puzzle: each piece you place opens up opportunities to solve the rest, and finishing a task means you know more than before.

column1: Who was MacArthur Wheeler?
column2: A man who robbed a bank in 1995 with lemon juice on his face, believing it made him invisible to cameras.

column1: What did MacArthur Wheeler say when arrested?
column2: But I wore the juice.

column1: Who studied Wheeler and named the effect?
column2: David Dunning and Justin Kruger.

column1: State the Dunning-Kruger effect.
column2: People with low ability at a task tend to paradoxically overestimate themselves.

column1: What are the axes of the Dunning-Kruger curve?
column2: Confidence against competence or knowledge.

column1: What is Mount Stupid?
column2: The early peak of high confidence based on very little knowledge.

column1: What is the Valley of Despair?
column2: The low point where increased knowledge has collapsed your confidence.

column1: What is the internal monologue at Mount Stupid?
column2: I know everything about this.

column1: What is the internal monologue in the Valley of Despair?
column2: I'll never understand this!

column1: What are the two ways people get stuck on the Dunning-Kruger curve?
column2: Stopping early and keeping a false sense of mastery, or quitting in the Valley believing they learned nothing.

column1: In the debate illustration, who wins the popular vote and why?
column2: The simpleton, because he is confident and people tend to trust certainty.

column1: Why does the good student stay quiet in the debate example?
column2: She knows more but does not realise it, and lacks confidence.

column1: What cultural variation was cited for self-assessment?
column2: 93% of Americans think they are above-average drivers, versus 69% of Swedes; Japanese people tend to underestimate their ability.

column1: What Socrates quote closes the Dunning-Kruger material?
column2: I know that I am intelligent because I know that I know nothing.

column1: Why should you be worried if you do NOT feel imposter syndrome starting a project?
column2: It suggests you did not understand the project, or lack the knowledge to see what lies ahead - you may be on Mount Stupid.

column1: How do imposter syndrome and Dunning-Kruger relate?
column2: They are opposite states: imposter syndrome means you can see the size of the problem; Dunning-Kruger means you cannot see it yet.

column1: Which of imposter syndrome and Dunning-Kruger is treated as desirable?
column2: Imposter syndrome is normal and good; Dunning-Kruger is called completely wrong.

column1: What assessment approach governs Gen AI use in this course?
column2: The Two-Lane Approach, as Lane 2: uncontrolled assessment.

column1: State pillar 1 of Gen AI use.
column2: If GenAI contributed significantly to a code block or report section, you must disclose it; failure is investigated as plagiarism.

column1: State pillar 2 of Gen AI use.
column2: Every student is 100% responsible for every line of code and every paragraph, regardless of who or what authored it.

column1: What happens if you cannot explain code in the Q&A?
column2: You are graded as if you do not understand the material, even if AI or a teammate wrote it.

column1: Why is a "black box" excuse rejected?
column2: Because it is not an acceptable engineering justification - an explanation you cannot give is one you do not have.

column1: State pillar 3 of Gen AI use.
column2: Generating complete code with AI or copying from a prompt is prohibited and scores zero; primarily AI-authored work may trigger disciplinary action.

column1: What is AI reportedly good and bad at, per the lecturer?
column2: Very good with UI, very bad with backend code; it does not understand quality.

column1: What workflow is required if you use AI-generated code?
column2: Refactor it into the proper structure, peer review it before it reaches the default branch, and return it to the developer if quality is low.

column1: Why does poor code quality cost more than its own 15 marks?
column2: Because quality feeds the holistic score, which drags down the entire project mark.
